title: How vaccines train the immune system

verified.text: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless version or piece of a germ: a weakened or killed germ, a protein from it, or genetic instructions (as in mRNA vaccines) for the body to make that protein.
The immune system treats that piece as an invader: B cells make antibodies that latch onto it, and T cells help coordinate the response and destroy infected cells.
After the response, long-lived memory B and T cells remain, so if the real germ arrives later the body recognises it and responds much faster.
Some vaccines need booster doses to keep the immune memory strong.
In 1796 Edward Jenner showed that material from cowpox could protect a person from smallpox, the first vaccine.
Smallpox was declared eradicated worldwide by the WHO in 1980.
India was certified polio-free by the WHO in 2014, as part of the South-East Asia region.
When enough people are immune, a germ struggles to spread, which also protects people who cannot be vaccinated; this is called herd immunity.

knownErrors.correction: Large studies found no link between vaccines and autism.
